subject: chemistry
title: Unit 1 practice exam
summary: A 75-minute exam-style test on all of Unit 1, with six short-answer questions and full worked solutions plus 20 multiple-choice questions on atoms, bonding, the mole, organic chemistry, polymers and green chemistry.
body:
This practice exam tests everything in Year 11 Chemistry Unit 1, in the same style as a school exam: short-answer questions where you show your working, and multiple-choice questions. It is the best way to find out what you really know before the real thing.

## How to use this practice exam

- **Time limit:** 75 minutes in total. Spend about 50 minutes on the short-answer questions (39 marks) and about 25 minutes on the 20 multiple-choice questions (20 marks).
- **Conditions:** work alone, with no notes. You may use a scientific calculator, a periodic table and the VCE data book.
- **Use these values:** Avogadro constant Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. Relative atomic masses: H 1.0, C 12.0, N 14.0, O 16.0, Na 23.0, Cl 35.5, Ca 40.1, Br 79.9.
- Write your short answers on paper first, then check them against the worked solutions. Be honest when you mark: a correct answer with no working usually loses marks in a real exam.
- Then do the multiple-choice questions below. Read every explanation, including for the ones you got right.
- Make a list of the topics you lost marks on and go back to those lessons.

## Topics covered

- Atomic structure, isotopes and relative atomic mass
- Electron configurations, core charge and periodic trends
- Metallic bonding, the reactivity series and alloys
- Ionic bonding, formulas, names and properties
- Covalent bonding, Lewis structures, VSEPR shapes and polarity
- Covalent network lattices and intermolecular forces
- The mole, molar mass, percentage composition, empirical and molecular formulas
- Hydrocarbons and organic families, naming up to C8
- Addition and condensation polymers, LDPE and HDPE, thermoplastics and thermosets
- Green chemistry principles, circular economy and atom economy

## Short-answer questions

### Question 1 (6 marks)

Copper has two naturally occurring isotopes, ⁶³Cu (relative isotopic mass 62.93) and ⁶⁵Cu (relative isotopic mass 64.93). The relative atomic mass of copper is 63.55.

a. Write the full electron configuration of a copper atom (Z = 29). (1 mark)

b. Calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope. (3 marks)

c. Copper is used for electrical wiring. Use the electron-sea model to explain why copper conducts electricity and why it can be drawn into a wire. (2 marks)

### Question 2 (8 marks)

A student tested four solid substances, W, X, Y and Z.

| Substance | Melting point (°C) | Conducts as a solid? | Conducts when molten? |
|---|---|---|---|
| W | 2852 | no | yes |
| X | 1710 | no | no |
| Y | −182 | no | no |
| Z | 660 | yes | yes |

a. Name the type of bonding or structure in each substance: metallic, ionic, covalent network or covalent molecular. (4 marks)

b. Explain why W conducts electricity when molten but not when solid. (2 marks)

c. Explain why Y has such a low melting point. (2 marks)

### Question 3 (7 marks)

Water (H₂O) boils at 100 °C, but hydrogen sulfide (H₂S), a molecule of similar shape, boils at about −60 °C.

a. State the shape of the H₂S molecule and explain how VSEPR theory predicts it. (2 marks)

b. Explain the large difference between the boiling points of H₂O and H₂S. Refer to the intermolecular forces in each. (3 marks)

c. Carbon dioxide contains polar C=O bonds, yet CO₂ is a non-polar molecule. Explain why. (2 marks)

### Question 4 (6 marks)

A sugar contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Its molar mass is 180 g mol⁻¹.

a. Find the empirical formula of the sugar. (3 marks)

b. Find its molecular formula. (1 mark)

c. Calculate the number of oxygen atoms in 4.50 g of the sugar. (2 marks)

### Question 5 (8 marks)

Ethanol can be made in two ways.

Route 1 (fermentation of sugar from plants):

`C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) → 2C₂H₅OH(aq) + 2CO₂(g)`

Route 2 (hydration of ethene from crude oil):

`C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) → C₂H₅OH(g)`

a. Give the systematic name of CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, an alcohol in the same homologous series as ethanol. (1 mark)

b. Ethanol reacts with ethanoic acid to form an ester. Name the ester. (1 mark)

c. Propene, CH₂=CHCH₃, forms a polymer. Name the type of polymerisation and draw the repeating unit. (2 marks)

d. Calculate the atom economy for producing ethanol by Route 1. (2 marks)

e. Using two different green chemistry principles, give one advantage of Route 1 and one advantage of Route 2. (2 marks)

### Question 6 (4 marks)

Milk bottles are made from high-density polyethene (HDPE), while cling wrap is made from low-density polyethene (LDPE).

a. Explain, in terms of structure and intermolecular forces, why HDPE is stiffer and stronger than LDPE. (2 marks)

b. Both HDPE and LDPE are thermoplastics. Explain what this means and why it makes them suitable for recycling by remelting. (2 marks)

## Worked solutions

### Question 1

a. `1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s¹` (1 mark). Copper is an exception: one 4s electron moves to give a full 3d¹⁰ subshell. Writing 3d⁹ 4s² does not earn the mark.

b. Let the fraction of ⁶³Cu be x, so the fraction of ⁶⁵Cu is (1 − x). (1 mark for setting up)

`62.93x + 64.93(1 − x) = 63.55`

`64.93 − 2.00x = 63.55`

`2.00x = 1.38`, so `x = 0.690` (1 mark)

Abundances: ⁶³Cu = **69.0%** and ⁶⁵Cu = **31.0%** (1 mark).

Check: (62.93 × 69.0 + 64.93 × 31.0) ÷ 100 = (4342.17 + 2012.83) ÷ 100 = 63.55. Correct, and it makes sense that the lighter isotope is more abundant because 63.55 is closer to 62.93.

c. Copper is a lattice of Cu cations in a sea of delocalised electrons. The delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice, so they carry charge when a voltage is applied (1 mark). The attraction between the cations and the electron sea acts in all directions (non-directional), so layers of cations can slide past each other without the bonding breaking, which lets copper be drawn into wire (1 mark).

### Question 2

a. (1 mark each)
- W: **ionic** (high melting point; conducts only when molten).
- X: **covalent network** (very high melting point; never conducts).
- Y: **covalent molecular** (very low melting point; never conducts).
- Z: **metallic** (conducts as a solid and a liquid).

b. W is an ionic lattice of positive and negative ions. In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions, so they cannot move to carry charge (1 mark). When molten, the lattice breaks down and the ions are free to move, so the liquid conducts (1 mark).

c. Y is made of separate molecules. Melting only has to overcome the weak intermolecular forces between molecules; the strong covalent bonds inside the molecules do not break (1 mark). Because these forces are weak, little energy is needed, so the melting point is low (1 mark).

### Question 3

a. **Bent (V-shaped)** (1 mark). The central S atom has four electron groups: two bonding pairs and two lone pairs. These repel each other and spread out tetrahedrally, but the shape is named from the atoms only, giving a bent molecule (1 mark).

b.
- Water has an H atom bonded directly to the highly electronegative O atom, so strong hydrogen bonds form between water molecules (1 mark).
- S is much less electronegative than O, so H₂S cannot form hydrogen bonds; its molecules are held only by dispersion forces and weaker dipole–dipole attractions (1 mark).
- Much more energy is needed to separate water molecules, so water boils at a much higher temperature, even though H₂S has more electrons (1 mark).

c. CO₂ is a linear molecule (two electron groups around C, no lone pairs) (1 mark). The two C=O bond dipoles are equal in size and point in opposite directions, so they cancel and there is no overall dipole (1 mark).

### Question 4

a. Assume 100 g, so 40.0 g C, 6.7 g H and 53.3 g O.

| | C | H | O |
|---|---|---|---|
| mass (g) | 40.0 | 6.7 | 53.3 |
| moles = m ÷ M | 40.0 ÷ 12.0 = 3.33 | 6.7 ÷ 1.0 = 6.7 | 53.3 ÷ 16.0 = 3.33 |
| ÷ smallest (3.33) | 1.00 | 2.0 | 1.00 |

Moles calculated correctly (1 mark); ratio found (1 mark); empirical formula **CH₂O** (1 mark).

b. Empirical formula mass = 12.0 + 2(1.0) + 16.0 = 30.0 g mol⁻¹. Multiplier = 180 ÷ 30.0 = 6. Molecular formula **C₆H₁₂O₆** (1 mark).

c. M(C₆H₁₂O₆) = 6(12.0) + 12(1.0) + 6(16.0) = 72.0 + 12.0 + 96.0 = 180.0 g mol⁻¹

`n(C₆H₁₂O₆) = m ÷ M = 4.50 ÷ 180.0 = 0.0250 mol` (1 mark)

`n(O atoms) = 6 × 0.0250 = 0.150 mol`

`N(O) = n × Nₐ = 0.150 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 9.03 × 10²² atoms` (1 mark, three significant figures)

### Question 5

a. **Propan-1-ol** (1 mark). Three carbons (prop-) and the –OH on carbon 1.

b. **Ethyl ethanoate** (1 mark). The alcohol part (ethyl) comes first and the acid part (ethanoate) second.

c. **Addition polymerisation** (1 mark). The repeating unit is –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–, with bonds extending from each end and the CH₃ group as a side branch (1 mark). The polymer is polypropene.

d. M(C₆H₁₂O₆) = 180.0 g mol⁻¹; M(C₂H₅OH) = 2(12.0) + 6(1.0) + 16.0 = 46.0 g mol⁻¹

`Atom economy = (2 × 46.0) ÷ 180.0 × 100 = 92.0 ÷ 180.0 × 100 = 51.1%` (1 mark for using the coefficient 2, 1 mark for the answer)

e. Any two different principles, one for each route (1 mark each):
- Route 1 uses a **renewable feedstock** (sugar from plants) rather than crude oil, and it runs at low temperature, giving better **energy efficiency**.
- Route 2 has an **atom economy** of 100% because ethanol is the only product, so no atoms are wasted as by-products.

### Question 6

a. HDPE chains have very little branching, so they can pack closely together (1 mark). Closely packed chains have more contact, so the dispersion forces between chains are stronger, making HDPE stiffer, stronger and denser than branched LDPE, whose chains cannot pack closely (1 mark).

b. A thermoplastic has no covalent cross-links between its chains, so it softens and melts when heated as the forces between chains are overcome (1 mark). This means it can be melted and reshaped into new products many times, which is what mechanical recycling needs (1 mark).

questions.prompt: The isotopes ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl differ in their:
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same atomic number (17 protons) but different mass numbers, so ³⁵Cl has 18 neutrons and ³⁷Cl has 20. Option C is tempting, but isotopes have the same electron arrangement and so the same chemical properties.

questions.prompt: An atom has the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴. Where is it in the periodic table?
questions.explanation: The highest occupied shell is 3, so it is in period 3. It has 6 valence electrons (3s² 3p⁴), which places it in group 16 (it is sulfur). Option B is tempting if you count only the 4 p electrons; option C counts valence electrons but uses the old group number and the wrong period.

questions.prompt: What is the core charge of a chlorine atom?
questions.explanation: Core charge = protons − inner-shell electrons = 17 − 10 = +7. Option A is the nuclear charge, which ignores shielding by the 10 inner electrons. Option D is the charge of the chloride ion, not the core charge.

questions.prompt: The first four ionisation energies of an element are approximately 738, 1451, 7733 and 10540 kJ mol⁻¹. Which group is the element most likely in?
questions.explanation: The big jump comes between the 2nd and 3rd ionisation energies, so after two electrons are removed the next must come from an inner shell. The element has 2 valence electrons and is in group 2 (these are magnesium's values). Option C is tempting if you count the number of values before the largest value instead of before the big jump.

questions.prompt: Why does electronegativity decrease down group 17?

options.A: Core charge decreases down the group.
options.B: The number of protons decreases down the group.
options.C: Atoms gain more neutrons, which shield the nucleus.
options.D: Core charge stays the same but the valence shell is further from the nucleus.

questions.explanation: Down the group, core charge stays at +7, but each element has an extra shell, so the bonding electrons are further from the nucleus and attracted less strongly. Option A is a common mistake: core charge is constant down a group, not decreasing. Neutrons have no charge and do not shield.

questions.prompt: Magnesium has a higher melting point than sodium. The best explanation is that magnesium:

options.A: forms 2+ ions and contributes two delocalised electrons per atom, so the metallic bonding is stronger
options.B: has a larger atomic radius than sodium
options.C: has stronger covalent bonds between its atoms
options.D: has more neutrons in its nucleus

questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ has a higher charge than Na⁺ and is smaller, and each Mg atom adds two electrons to the electron sea, so the attraction between cations and electrons is stronger and more energy is needed to melt it. Option B is wrong: Mg is smaller than Na because it is further across period 3. Metals do not have covalent bonding.

questions.prompt: A strip of metal X was placed in separate solutions of Cu²⁺, Pb²⁺ and Zn²⁺ ions. A coating formed in the Cu²⁺ and Pb²⁺ solutions, but there was no change in the Zn²⁺ solution. What is the order of reactivity, from most to least reactive?
questions.explanation: X displaces copper and lead, so it is more reactive than both. It does not displace zinc, so zinc is more reactive than X. That gives Zn, X, Pb, Cu, with Pb above Cu as in the reactivity series. Option A is tempting, but the absence of a reaction with Zn²⁺ shows that X is less reactive than zinc.

questions.prompt: Why is an alloy such as steel usually harder than the pure metal?

options.A: The alloy contains covalent bonds between atoms.
options.B: The alloy has fewer delocalised electrons.
options.C: The alloy contains ionic bonds that hold layers in place.
options.D: Atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide as easily.

questions.explanation: In a substitutional or interstitial alloy, atoms of a different size distort the lattice, so layers of cations no longer slide easily over each other. This makes the alloy harder and less malleable. Option B is tempting but the electron sea is still present; the key change is to how the layers move.

questions.prompt: What is the formula of iron(III) nitrate?
questions.explanation: Iron(III) is Fe³⁺ and nitrate is NO₃⁻, so three nitrate ions are needed for every iron ion, written with brackets: Fe(NO₃)₃. Option C puts the 3 in the wrong place: it would mean three iron ions. Option D treats the Roman numeral as a subscript pattern like Fe₂O₃.

questions.prompt: Why are ionic solids brittle?

options.A: When a layer shifts, ions of the same charge line up and repel, splitting the crystal.
options.B: The ionic bonds are weak and break easily.
options.C: Ionic solids contain delocalised electrons that move when struck.
options.D: Ionic compounds are made of separate molecules held by weak forces.

questions.explanation: A force can move one layer of ions so that positive ions sit next to positive ions and negative next to negative. The repulsion splits the crystal. Option B is tempting but wrong: ionic bonds are strong, which is why ionic compounds have high melting points.

questions.prompt: What is the shape of the methanal molecule, H₂CO, where carbon is the central atom with a double bond to oxygen?
questions.explanation: Carbon has three electron groups (two C–H single bonds and one C=O double bond, which counts as one group) and no lone pairs, so the shape is trigonal planar. Option B is tempting if you count the double bond as two groups, but a multiple bond counts as one electron group in VSEPR.

questions.prompt: Which molecule has polar bonds but is non-polar overall?
questions.explanation: CCl₄ is tetrahedral with four identical polar C–Cl bonds, so the dipoles cancel. CHCl₃ is the tempting option: it is also tetrahedral, but one C–H bond is different from the three C–Cl bonds, so the dipoles do not cancel and it is polar.

questions.prompt: Which of these substances has the highest boiling point?
questions.explanation: Methanol has hydrogen bonding between molecules (H bonded to O), which is much stronger than the dispersion forces holding the alkanes together, so it has the highest boiling point (it is a liquid at room temperature, while the three alkanes are gases). Option D is tempting because propane has the most electrons, but its dispersion forces are still weaker than methanol's hydrogen bonds.

questions.prompt: Graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not. Why?

options.A: In graphite each carbon is covalently bonded to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom.
options.B: Graphite contains ions that are free to move.
options.C: Diamond has weaker covalent bonds than graphite.
options.D: Graphite is a metal and diamond is a non-metal.

questions.explanation: Each C atom in graphite uses three electrons to bond within its layer; the fourth electron is delocalised along the layer and can carry charge. In diamond all four electrons are used in bonds. Option B is wrong because graphite contains no ions: it conducts by moving electrons.

questions.prompt: How many moles of carbon dioxide are in 8.80 g of CO₂?
questions.explanation: M(CO₂) = 12.0 + 2(16.0) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹, so n = m ÷ M = 8.80 ÷ 44.0 = 0.200 mol. Option A comes from dividing by the molar mass of carbon only (8.80 ÷ 12.0 = 0.733). Option D comes from multiplying instead of dividing.

questions.prompt: How many hydrogen atoms are in 0.250 mol of ethane, C₂H₆?
questions.explanation: Each molecule has 6 H atoms, so n(H) = 6 × 0.250 = 1.50 mol, and N = 1.50 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 9.03 × 10²³. Option A is the number of ethane molecules (0.250 × 6.02 × 10²³). Option D is the total number of atoms (8 per molecule).

questions.prompt: What is the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃?
questions.explanation: M(NH₄NO₃) = 2(14.0) + 4(1.0) + 3(16.0) = 80.0 g mol⁻¹. There are two N atoms, so %N = 28.0 ÷ 80.0 × 100 = 35.0%. Option A counts only one N atom. Option D is the percentage of oxygen.

questions.prompt: What is the systematic name of CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The chain has five carbons (pent-) and a C=C double bond, so it is an alkene (-ene). Numbering from the end nearest the double bond puts it between C2 and C3, giving pent-2-ene. Option A numbers from the wrong end; the lowest possible number must be used.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a thermosetting polymer?

options.A: Its chains are held only by dispersion forces, so it softens when heated.
options.B: It is always made from renewable feedstocks.
options.C: It is made by addition polymerisation of alkenes only.
options.D: Its chains are joined by covalent cross-links, so it does not soften when heated.

questions.explanation: Thermosets have strong covalent cross-links between chains, so heating cannot let the chains slide past each other; instead the polymer chars or decomposes. Option A describes a thermoplastic, which is the most common mix-up.

questions.prompt: Ethanol can be made from bromoethane: `CH₃CH₂Br + NaOH → CH₃CH₂OH + NaBr`. What is the atom economy for producing ethanol? (Use H 1.0, C 12.0, O 16.0, Na 23.0, Br 79.9.)
questions.explanation: M(CH₃CH₂Br) = 2(12.0) + 5(1.0) + 79.9 = 108.9; M(NaOH) = 23.0 + 16.0 + 1.0 = 40.0; total reactants = 148.9 g mol⁻¹. M(CH₃CH₂OH) = 46.0 g mol⁻¹. Atom economy = 46.0 ÷ 148.9 × 100 = 30.9%. Option B divides by the bromoethane only and forgets the NaOH. Option D is the percentage that ends up as the by-product NaBr.
